ann_10.text: Through this part, working in protective service lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 61% to about 48% (on the training data only).
Across the whole model, protective service work changes it only slightly compared with a professional job.

ann_11.text: Through this part, being born in Poland raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 61% to about 66% (on the training data only).
In the training data, 70 people were born in Poland.

ann_12.text: Through this part, being born in India slightly raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 61% to about 63% (on the training data only).
In the training data, 119 people were born in India.

ann_13.text: Through this part, serving in the armed forces lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 61% to about 52% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this).
Only 12 people in the training data serve in the armed forces.

ann_14.text: Through this part, being born in Portugal lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 61% to about 38% (on the training data only).
In the training data, 49 people were born in Portugal.

ann_15.text: Through this part, being born in Laos raises a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less from about 61% to above 99% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this).
Only 17 people in the training data were born in Laos.

ann_17.text: Through this part, a higher education level and higher capital losses clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less steadily: from about 80% at 7 to about 38% at 13 on the 1-16 scale, and from about 61% at 0 to about 31% at 1887 US dollars.

A missing work class or being never married clearly raises it to about 96%, other ways of not being married to about 94%, farming or fishing to about 87%, other service work to about 86% and being a woman to about 76%.
A missing occupation clearly lowers it to about 24%, being a wife to about 33%, not living in a family to about 48% and an executive or managerial job to about 54%.
Being older and working longer hours clearly lower it steadily: from about 69% at 22 to about 47% at 58 years, and from about 71% at 24 to about 50% at 55 hours a week.

Being born in Colombia raises it to about 99%, in Peru to about 82%, in Thailand to about 79% and in Mexico to about 76%, while being born in Ireland lowers it to about 34%, and having 1st-4th grade as the highest education to about 39% (on the training data only).
Never having worked raises it to above 99% and working without pay to about 79% (the model has little data on this: only 9 and 17 people).
Preschool or 9th-grade education and being born in France, Cuba or Germany change it only slightly (on the training data only), as do technical support work and the other work classes.

ann_18.text: This part holds the inputs the model never connected; switching it off makes no difference to the predictions.

ann_19.text: Across the whole model, higher capital gains clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less slowly at first, then faster: from about 61% at 0 to about 10% at 6849 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.
A higher education level and higher capital losses clearly lower it steadily: from about 80% at 7 to about 38% at 13 on the 1-16 scale, and from about 61% at 0 to about 31% at 1887 US dollars.

Compared with being married to a civilian spouse, being never married clearly raises it to about 96%, and being married with the spouse absent or otherwise not married to about 94%; being a woman clearly raises it to about 76%.

Compared with a professional job in the private sector, a missing work class clearly raises it to about 96%, farming or fishing to about 87%, other service work to about 86% and self-employment (not incorporated) to about 74%, while a missing occupation clearly lowers it to about 24%.
Being older and working longer hours clearly lower it steadily: from about 69% at 22 to about 47% at 58 years, and from about 71% at 24 to about 50% at 55 hours a week.
Being a wife (about 33%) or not living in a family (about 48%) rather than a husband also clearly lowers it.

Country of birth moves it a lot for a few countries: about 99% for people born in Colombia, about 82% for Peru, about 79% for Thailand and about 76% for Mexico, against about 34% for Ireland and about 38% for Portugal (on the training data only).
Being born in Laos raises it to above 99% (on the training data only; the model has little data on this, with only 17 people), and the model ignores the census sampling weight.

ann_8.text: Through this part, higher capital gains clearly lower a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less slowly at first, then faster: from about 61% at 0 to about 10% at 6849 US dollars, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.

They lower it only once they rise above about 3511 US dollars: for the typical person this part acts on (the same 37-year-old married man with no capital gains), going from 0 to 5013 US dollars clearly lowers it from about 61% to about 35%.
In the training data, 2387 of the 39073 people this applies to are already past that point.

The drop clearly depends on country of birth: from about 61% to about 10% for people born anywhere other than the Netherlands, Italy, Jamaica, China or Scotland, but only to about 58% for people born in Italy.
Through this part, being born in Italy, China or Scotland changes it only slightly (on the training data only; the model has little data on this for Scotland, with only 16 people).

ann_9.text: Through this part, being married with the spouse absent slightly lowers a typical person's predicted chance of an income of $50,000 or less, from about 61% to about 59% (on the training data only).
Switching this part off makes almost no difference to the predictions.

ann_8.original: Rectified multi-stage pipeline transforming capital-gain (-63). Capital-gain fans through a depth-3 ReLU cascade (3446->4739->2129 plus direct) converging on hub 655, read out to the output via four opposing-sign weights (655/313 vs 5102/6421). The depth-3 structure therefore exceeds the single threshold it produces over the data - excess structure, the same phenomenon as the fused native-country terms below. summary.text: For a typical person (a 37-year-old White married man born in the United States, a high-school graduate in a professional job in the private sector, working 40 hours a week, with no capital gains or losses), the model predicts about a 61% chance of an income of $50,000 or less, and higher capital gains clearly lower that slowly at first, then faster: from about 61% at none to about 10% at 6849 US dollars, a large change, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted chance cannot go much lower.
A higher education level clearly lowers the predicted chance steadily: from about 80% at 7 to about 38% at 13 on the 1-16 scale.
Being never married rather than married, or having a missing work class, clearly raises it to about 96%, while a missing occupation clearly lowers it to about 24%.

Capital gains lower it only once they rise above about 3511 US dollars, so slowly at first, then faster, and the drop clearly depends on country of birth: from about 61% to about 10% for people born anywhere other than the Netherlands, Italy, Jamaica, China or Scotland, but only to about 58% for people born in Italy.
The model ignores the census sampling weight.
